ety.text: Uncertain. From either: * Earlier English roger (“a begging vagabond who pretends to be a poor scholar from Oxford or Cambridge”), possibly from Latin rogō (“to ask”). * Middle French rogue (“arrogant, haughty”), from Old Northern French rogre (“aggressive”), from Old Norse hrokr (“excess, exuberance”), for which see Icelandic hroki (“arrogance”), though OED does not document this. * Celtic; see Breton rog (“haughty”).

senses.d: A scoundrel, rascal or unprincipled, deceitful, and unreliable person.
ex: And meet time it was, when yon usher, vinegar-faced rogue that he is, began to inquire what popish trangam you were wearing […]

senses.d: A mischievous scamp.
ex: Ah, you sweet little rogue, you!

senses.d: A vagrant.
Malware that deceitfully presents itself as antispyware.
An aggressive animal separate from the herd, especially an elephant.
ex: If he is a rogue, and there's any truth to territoriality at all, we got a good chance of spotting him between Cape Scott and South Beach.

senses.d: A horse, mule, or donkey that is difficult to control; a refractory horse, especially a racehorse.
ex: The rogues among the horses and mules sought every chance to break the line and hide under shady trees where sweet grass grew.

senses.d: A plant that shows some undesirable variation.
A character class focusing on stealthy conduct.
Vicious and solitary.
Large, destructive and unpredictable.
Deceitful, unprincipled.
Mischievous, unpredictable.
To cull; to destroy plants not meeting a required standard, especially when saving seed, rogue or unwanted plants are removed before pollination.
To cheat.
ex: And then to think that Mark should have rogued me of five shiners! He was clever—that's a fact.

senses.d: To give the name or designation of rogue to; to decry.
ex: he Atheists may endeavour to rogue and ridicule all incorporeal Substance

senses.d: To wander; to play the vagabond; to play knavish tricks.
ex: if hee be but once so taken idlely roguing

From Roger, used circa 1940 in UK and US military communication to represent "R" when spelling out a word. "R" is the first letter in received, used to acknowledge understanding a message. "Roger" for "received" was in spoken usage in air traffic radio parlance by 1950.
Possibly from Old High German Hrotger via Shelta roger.

senses.d: Received (used in radio communications to acknowledge that a message has been received and understood)
To acknowledge by saying "roger".
ex: The Explorer radio operator rogered receipt of the War Room's signal.

senses.d: Of a man, to have sexual intercourse with (someone), especially in a rough manner.
To have sexual intercourse.
ex: Should not a Half-pay Officer roger for sixpence?

senses.d: An act of sexual intercourse.
ex: ALAN: Lynn, if I have to put back my roger with Sonja one more time, I'll be fit to burst.
